changes.name: The First Fog
changes.entry: The first heavy fog of the year is treated as a living visitor: the Fog Mother. Until noon, all Fogport speaks only in whispers, shutters its mirrors, and keeps children indoors, lest the fog learn a name worth carrying away.

changes.name: Feast of the Drowned Bride
changes.entry: Unmarried women wear sea-green ribbons; bachelors carry hooded lanterns from the quay to the old sea wall. A couple who kisses before sunrise is publicly expected to marry before winter—or explain themselves to both families.

changes.name: Blackwake Pardon
changes.entry: Blackwake’s clerks traditionally overlook ordinary pickpocketing for one day. A thief caught in the act must buy the victim supper before sunset, then give a sworn account of exactly how the theft was managed.

changes.name: The Hungry Bells
changes.entry: Church bells, tram bells, and factory bells ring whenever a death is reported. No one counts aloud. The superstition says that if the final number is spoken, one of the bells will answer with a dead person’s voice.

changes.name: The Widow’s Ball
changes.entry: Widows host the season’s first dance and choose their partners without permission or negotiation. To refuse an invitation is said to invite seven years of loneliness; most men find a way to be charming.

changes.name: Grig Ascension
changes.entry: Within specially blessed districts, Grigs ceremonially remove their Grig Tack and speak or dream unbound for one night. Human guests lower their eyes—not merely from respect, but from fear of what a barefaced Grig might see in them.

changes.name: Crab King’s Market
changes.entry: Crabbers release hundreds of enormous sea crabs into the market streets. Anyone who catches one barehanded keeps it, provided they carry it home alive and do not complain when it learns the route back.

changes.name: Festival of Borrowed Faces
changes.entry: Everyone wears a mask modeled after someone else: neighbors, enemies, saints, dead relatives, or badly disguised officials. Lovers often meet as strangers and are not meant to admit themselves until midnight.

changes.name: Rain Marriage
changes.entry: If rain falls before noon, every engaged couple in Fogport is expected to marry that day, however unfinished the dress, feast, ring, or argument. A rain-marriage is considered blessed; postponement is considered a challenge to the weather.

changes.name: Night of Empty Chairs
changes.entry: Every household leaves one chair set with a plate and cup for a forgotten ancestor, wandering monster, or unexpected friend. In the morning, nobody asks who occupied it—especially if the plate is clean and the chair is wet.

changes.name: The Great Molting
changes.entry: Children wear paper feathers while adults shed old clothes into huge communal nests built in alleys and courtyards. By dawn the nests are burned, stolen, or picked clean, and last year’s failures are supposed to be gone with them.

changes.name: Lantern Court
changes.entry: Minor disputes are judged publicly beneath strings of lanterns, often by a rotating jury of shopkeepers and drunks. The loser buys drinks, both sides embrace, and any later grudge becomes a new case next year.

changes.name: Lovers Lost in Fog
changes.entry: Couples deliberately separate in the thickest fog they can find and attempt to return to one another before dawn. Success promises lifelong devotion. Failure does not end a romance, but it gives every aunt in Fogport something to discuss.

changes.name: Feast of a Thousand Teeth
changes.entry: Barbers, surgeons, and tooth-pullers work without charge while families hang carved wooden teeth above their doors. The teeth are meant to discourage hungry spirits, Gutterkin, and anything that might otherwise test a sleeping household.

changes.name: The Gull Parliament
changes.entry: No gull may be chased away, fed on purpose, or insulted today. Dockside interpreters read their fights, flights, thefts, and drownings as predictions of weather, politics, and the fate of incoming ships.

changes.name: King’s Beggar Day
changes.entry: The wealthy dress as paupers, while beggars are seated at banquet tables in borrowed finery. Everyone pretends not to recognize anyone else. Civic Vigilance officers are notably absent—or dressed too well to be identified.

changes.name: Festival of Honest Ghosts
changes.entry: Each citizen confesses one shame to a complete stranger before sunrise. The secret is believed to pass to the dead, who carry it safely out to sea. Most people choose a stranger they will never meet again.

changes.name: The Monster Census
changes.entry: Citizens decorate tolerable monsters with ribbons while city clerks attempt to count every creature living in Fogport. The resulting total is treated as official until the next monstrous incident makes the previous number embarrassing.

changes.name: Sea Funeral
changes.entry: Families whose dead were never recovered launch empty coffins onto the Sayir Sea. They drink, sing, and celebrate until dawn as though death has finally accepted the body it was owed.

changes.name: Long Night of Lanterns
changes.entry: Every Fogport window displays a lantern. If one goes dark unexpectedly, neighbors arrive without invitation carrying food, weapons, and spare candles. No one asks what happened until the light is steady again.
